The Common dab (Limanda limanda) is a commercially important flatfish that exhibits determinate growth, with females reaching an ultimate total length of 40 cm [Li = 40 cm]. Newly hatched larvae emerge from pelagic eggs measuring approximately 0.93 mm in diameter, and the corresponding wet weight at birth has been estimated at 0.0004 grams [Wwb = 0.0004 grams], a value derived from the volumetric relationship of a sphere with the egg's radius. This minuscule initial mass reflects the limited yolk reserves available to the endotrophic larva before it must transition to exogenous feeding. Field surveys across the North Sea indicate that the onset of sexual maturation occurs when individuals attain a total length at puberty of 26 cm [Lp = 26 cm], a size that is typically reached after several years of somatic growth. The trajectory from the lecithotrophic larval stage to the benthic juvenile phase involves a pronounced allometric shift during metamorphosis, after which the immature fish settles onto sandy substrates to commence its demersal existence. Growth rates during the juvenile period are highly variable and depend strongly on local food availability and bottom temperature.

Reproductive output in Limanda limanda has been quantified under controlled laboratory conditions that mimic the thermal regime of its natural habitat. At a stable water temperature of 9 °C [T = 9 °C], females produce a reproductive rate expressed through a combination of clutch size and spawning frequency: each female releases approximately 2,575 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 2,575 eggs per spawning event], and these events occur roughly once per day [F_R_i = events occur roughly once per day], yielding a daily rate of approximately 2,575 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 2,575 eggs per day]. This high fecundity is typical of many pleuronectiform species that broadcast spawn pelagic eggs into an unpredictable environment, where larval mortality rates are extremely high. The wet weight at puberty, which is the body mass corresponding to the size at which 50 percent of the population becomes reproductively mature, has been calculated from length-weight relationships as approximately 202 grams [Wwp = approximately 202 grams], a figure consistent with empirical data from the southern North Sea. Spawning aggregations form in deeper waters during the winter months, and individual females may migrate considerable distances to reach suitable spawning grounds.

The ultimate female wet weight represents the maximum body mass attainable by a fully grown individual under optimal conditions, and for Limanda limanda this asymptotic value has been estimated at 1,000 grams [Wwi = 1,000 grams]. This mass corresponds to the upper end of the size range observed in commercial catches from the central North Sea, where older females dominate the largest length classes. The relationship between length and weight in this species follows a power law, and the mass at puberty of 202 grams [Wwp = 202 grams] aligns well with the predicted value from the commonly used equation employing a coefficient of 0.00854 and an exponent of 3.091. The energetic investment in gonadal tissue is substantial for a fish of this size; gravid individuals may allocate a significant proportion of their somatic reserves to vitellogenesis prior to the spawning season. Comparisons with other pleuronectids, such as the plaice (Pleuronectes platessa), reveal that the common dab achieves a somewhat smaller maximum body size but compensates with a higher relative fecundity. This trade-off between somatic growth and reproductive output is a central feature of its life-history strategy.

Longevity data from otolith-based age determinations indicate that the maximum lifespan of Limanda limanda under natural conditions is approximately 12 years [am = approximately 12 years], a figure that was derived from samples collected in waters with an average bottom temperature of 9 °C [T = 9 °C]. This lifespan is intermediate among North Sea flatfishes; it is shorter than that of the long-lived halibut but exceeds the typical longevity of the more rapidly maturing solenette. The age structure of exploited populations shows that very few individuals survive beyond their tenth year, as fishing mortality removes most age classes before they reach natural senescence. The pelagic larval phase, which lasts several weeks, is a critical bottleneck in the life cycle, and the transition to the benthic juvenile stage occurs after a period of rapid morphological transformation. Mortality during the yolk-sac larva and early exotrophic stages is exceptionally high, with losses often exceeding 99 percent before settlement. Those individuals that successfully recruit to the juvenile population then face a prolonged period of growth on sandy bottoms before attaining sexual maturity.

The physiological ecology of Limanda limanda is shaped by its adaptation to cool, temperate waters, and many of its life-history traits have been characterized at the species' typical thermal optimum. The reproductive rate, for instance, was measured at the same ambient temperature of 9 °C [T = 9 °C] that also defines the conditions under which maximum longevity was recorded (12 years) [am = 12 years]. This temperature is typical of the southern North Sea during the peak spawning season and represents a thermal regime that balances the energetic costs of gamete production against the availability of planktonic food for the larvae. The species exhibits a typical iteroparous breeding pattern, with individuals spawning annually once they have attained the required body size. The ultimate total length of 40 cm [Li = 40 cm] is seldom achieved in heavily fished areas, where the average size of landed fish is considerably smaller. Comparative studies with populations from the Baltic Sea suggest that there may be local adaptation in growth rates and size at maturity, but the fundamental life-history parameters described here appear to be broadly representative of the species across its range.
